extract.title: Pay for the People Who Check: A Manifesto for Sustaining Human Knowledge

principles.statement: The scarce resource is the people who check, so fund checkers (fellowships, mentoring, tools, credit, legal defence for sleuths) rather than tokens, paying carefully so pay does not erode volunteer motivation.
Funders and provosts should stop counting outputs by a committed date, avoid substitute metrics, and credit curation, correction, maintenance, data sharing, mentoring and negative results.

AI answers used in scholarship must show representative sources, accurate citations, checkable open links and flags for thin evidence, with retraction checks at citation, stable shared pages and disclosed link-hallucination rates.
Checking must be checkable: no auditor paid by the count, no lab grading itself, auditor access to training checkpoints and retired models, findable funding, and a public no-fee audit layer.

Design the settings where claims are met, hiding cheap credibility cues and surfacing expensive ones, without penalizing language-barrier users, and measure human oversight rather than assuming it works.

Institutions must ensure competence precedes reliance on tools, practising and measuring oversight without tools, teaching programming before coding agents, with employers sharing this duty and a removal study funded.
Independence checks should examine who seeded corpora and who staffs checking roles, a commons of negative knowledge should be commissioned, and tail work funded independently of usage.

AI firms that use the commons must pay its infrastructure costs through deals with reporting and audit clauses, separate training and grounding controls, collective bargaining rights for producers, and multiple funders.

Every rule should name a policer, paymaster, review date and accountable outside overruler, with recipients committing to openness and forkability, dated self-assessments, Global South partners from the start, and funded refusal.

commitments: Those who sign contracts will write sourcing tests, retraction checks at citation and funder disclosure into procurement.
Name a payer, a steward and a review date for every item, and label claims that rest on models, reporting or single audits.
Reconvene in a year to check whether the money arrived.
OpenAttribution will co-govern with SciELO and Redalyc and publish a dated self-audit.
OpenAlex will publish a dated self-audit, run a working non-US mirror, and rank no evaluators.
System will make no patent claims on its findings standard and will publish a dated self-audit.
Wikimedia will publish its own edge logs.
Fund a tool-removal study in both orders, a field test of explain-first designs, a test of removing the first-person "I," and a longitudinal test of lateral reading before any mandate.
Give this manifesto its own review date so caution does not harden into unrevisited rules.

dissents.name: Sherry Turkle
dissents.position: The manifesto asks only how to integrate AI, not whether it belongs, and should keep AI out of therapy, grief and children's companionship and bar personas in paid tools.

dissents.name: Amy Brand
dissents.position: Open for reading is not open for training, so training should require author consent and retrieval should be favoured over pre-training.

dissents.name: Selena Deckelmann
dissents.position: Disagrees with Amy Brand's position that training should require author consent.

dissents.name: Katherine Maher
dissents.position: Disagrees with Amy Brand's position that training should require author consent.

dissents.name: Jason Priem
dissents.position: Disagrees with Amy Brand's position that training should require author consent.

dissents.name: Benjamin Bratton
dissents.position: Content should not be metered at all; a sovereign-wealth-style public dividend beats per-work licensing and micropayments.

dissents.name: Adam Becker
dissents.position: Checker and journalism money should come from public sources rather than voluntary lab money, and the manifesto should drop "AGI" and anthropomorphic verbs.

dissents.name: Peter Salib
dissents.position: Copyright should not become a welfare program; money should buy future scarce work via contracts, and courts should be the outside overruling body.

dissents.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
dissents.position: Human-only oversight at scale is theatre; the real question is auditors' independence, not whether they are machines.

dissents.name: David Weinberger
dissents.position: Declined to remove anthropomorphic verbs and calls these tools an epistemic gift as well as a risk.

dissents.name: Geoffrey Bilder
dissents.position: The word "AI" assumes the answers under debate, and he is suspicious nobody called his proposals wrong.

dissents.name: Ivan Oransky
dissents.position: Only stopping output counts addresses the source, a replacement metric may be unneeded, and reviewers asked to check more must be paid and given time.

dissents.name: Leslie Chan
dissents.position: The regime should be designed from the South with rankings removed from funding and promotion, as proposed mechanisms risk becoming "the next DOI."

dissents.name: Peter Pomerantsev
dissents.position: Designs assume good faith and usage markets reward seeding campaigns; identity registries endanger activists, and governance should center the reader's right to receive information.

dissents.name: Adrian Johns
dissents.position: Choke points get repurposed and courts cannot always be trusted, so the overseer question remains open, and the history of print's credibility should be corrected.

dissents.name: Tamar Gendler
dissents.position: Tying payment or credentials to learning or grounding events undermines intrinsic motivation, cutting against per-event payment, and humans-know/machines-predict distinctions are too tidy.

dissents.name: Ramón Alvarado
dissents.position: Only epistemic trust earned with warrants licenses trust in scientific uses, and human roles in the loop must be epistemically justified, not kept by default.

lead.why: The principle rests on scarcity: "The scarce resource is the people who check." It then calls for redirecting investment toward checking: "fund checkers ... rather than tokens." That matches the claim that verification, not production, is the bottleneck. It also overlaps with paying human labor, but the scarcity-and-reallocation framing is the main thrust.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Sherry Turkle
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent is about whether AI belongs in certain rooms at all. It says the manifesto "asks only how to integrate AI, not whether it belongs" and would keep AI out of "therapy, grief and children's companionship." This matches Turkle's position on the model_in_loop fault line. It says nothing about consent or payment.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Amy Brand
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent is about consent as the mechanism governing use of existing text: "training should require author consent." That is the opt-in position on the consent/payment fault line, set against open training. The preference for retrieval over pre-training follows from the same concern about how existing text gets used. It says nothing about whether a model belongs in the checking loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Selena Deckelmann
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent rejects "Amy Brand's position that training should require author consent." That is the consent/payment fault line: opt-in consent for training on existing text versus open training.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Katherine Maher
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent rejects "Amy Brand's position that training should require author consent." That is the consent/payment fault line: opt-in consent for training on existing text versus open training.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Jason Priem
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent rejects "Amy Brand's position that training should require author consent." That is the consent/payment fault line: opt-in consent for training on existing text versus open training.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Benjamin Bratton
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent is about how creators should be compensated. It argues "Content should not be metered at all" and favors "a sovereign-wealth-style public dividend" over "per-work licensing and micropayments." That is a position on the payment-mechanism fault line, not on whether a model belongs in the loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Adam Becker
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent argues that "Checker and journalism money should come from public sources rather than voluntary lab money" and asks to drop "AGI" and anthropomorphic verbs. That is a dispute over who funds public-interest work and over framing language. It is not about consent, levies or opt-in for training text versus open training, so it is not consent_or_payment. It also does not question whether a model belongs in the checking loop or the room, so it is not model_in_loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Peter Salib
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent rejects levy-style compensation for existing text ("Copyright should not become a welfare program") and argues money should instead "buy future scarce work via contracts." That matches the minority position on consent and payment: contracts for new work rather than dues or levies on existing text.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent is about whether models belong in the checking loop. It argues that "Human-only oversight at scale is theatre" and that what matters is "auditors' independence, not whether they are machines." That places it on the model-in-the-loop fault line (Becker, Turkle), taking the pro-machine side. It says nothing about consent or payment.

dissent_fault_lines.name: David Weinberger
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent concerns framing: it "Declined to remove anthropomorphic verbs" and calls the tools "an epistemic gift as well as a risk." It says nothing about consent or payment for training text. It also does not address whether a model belongs in the checking loop or the room. It is a disagreement over language and overall stance toward AI, so neither named fault line fits.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Geoffrey Bilder
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent objects that "The word 'AI' assumes the answers under debate" and voices suspicion that "nobody called his proposals wrong." These are complaints about terminology and about the lack of pushback in the process. It says nothing about consent, payment or levies, and nothing about whether a model belongs in the checking loop or the room.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Ivan Oransky
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent concerns research incentives and review labour: "Only stopping output counts addresses the source" and "reviewers asked to check more must be paid and given time." The payment it mentions is for reviewers, not a consent or compensation mechanism for training on text. It also does not question whether a model belongs in the checking loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Leslie Chan
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent is about designing the regime "from the South" and removing rankings from funding and promotion, warning that mechanisms risk becoming "the next DOI." That concerns global equity and incentive structures. It does not address consent/payment mechanisms for training data, and it does not address whether a model belongs in the checking loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Peter Pomerantsev
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent is about adversarial abuse and rights: "Designs assume good faith," "usage markets reward seeding campaigns," "identity registries endanger activists," and a call to "center the reader's right to receive information." It mentions usage markets only as a manipulation risk. It does not take a side on opt-in, levies or dues versus open training and pay-at-output, and it does not address whether a model belongs in the checking loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Adrian Johns
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent concerns who oversees the system: "Choke points get repurposed and courts cannot always be trusted, so the overseer question remains open". It also asks to correct "the history of print's credibility." It says nothing about opt-in, levies or payment for training text, nor about whether a model belongs in the checking loop, so neither named fault line fits.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Tamar Gendler
dissent_fault_lines.why: The objection is motivational crowding-out: "Tying payment or credentials to learning or grounding events undermines intrinsic motivation." It also rejects "humans-know/machines-predict distinctions" as "too tidy." It does not take a side on consent, opt-in, or levies for existing text versus open training, so it is not the consent_or_payment dispute. It also does not argue whether a model belongs in the checking loop or the room, so it is not model_in_loop.

dissent_fault_lines.name: Ramón Alvarado
dissent_fault_lines.why: The dissent concerns who belongs in the checking loop. It says "human roles in the loop must be epistemically justified, not kept by default," and that trust must be "earned with warrants." That is the same question about the composition of the verification loop, argued from the side opposite to Becker and Turkle. It has nothing to do with consent, levies or payment.
